# Integrated circuit and planar process (`integrated_circuit`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs semiconductors_transistor, semiconductor_purification; helped by photography, mosfet, boolean_logic
- Core idea: Instead of making transistors singly and wiring them by hand, make the whole circuit, transistors, resistors and connections, side by side in the surface of one slice of silicon. The planar process does it in repeated steps: grow an oxide layer on the slice, coat it with a light-sensitive lacquer, expose it through a photographic mask, etch windows in the oxide, diffuse dopants through the windows, re-oxidise, and finally evaporate aluminium and etch it into connecting tracks that run over the oxide. The oxide protects the junctions, and hundreds of identical circuits are made at once on one slice. Because everything is defined by photography, the patterns can be shrunk generation after generation, which is why the number of components per chip has doubled about every two years.
- Pitfalls:
  - Dust: one speck ruins a circuit, so the work needs filtered air and extreme cleanliness
  - Believing that many components on one chip must give a hopeless yield; this was the standard objection around 1960 and it proved wrong
  - Hydrofluoric acid, used to etch the oxide, causes deep burns and poisoning through the skin
  - Crediting a single inventor: Kilby's chip used wire bonds, Noyce's used Hoerni's planar process, and Dummer and Lehovec contributed essential ideas
- History: europe: 1952 – Dummer (Royal Radar Establishment) proposes a solid block circuit with no connecting wires; americas: 1955–1957 – Frosch and Derick show that an oxide layer masks selected dopants. At Bell Labs Jules Andrus and Walter Bond pattern openings in this layer with photoresist. Jay Lathrop and James Nall independently apply photoengraving to semiconductor fabrication. In September 1958 Kilby demonstrated his germanium circuit at Texas Instruments; 1959 Hoerni's planar process and Noyce's planar integrated circuit at Fairchild; 1965 Moore's observation on doubling; 1971 Intel 4004 microprocessor
- Read:
  - Jules Andrus, Fabrication of Semiconductor Devices, US patent 3,122,817 (filed 1957, granted 1964)
  - T. R. Reid, The Chip: How Two Americans Invented the Microchip and Launched a Revolution (1984)
  - Leslie Berlin, The Man Behind the Microchip: Robert Noyce and the Invention of Silicon Valley (2005)
